# `prefer-eql-over-order`

<!-- rule-docs:header (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
Tier: style · Profile: idiomatic · Default: off · Fixes: fix all · Options: none

Reports `std.mem.order(T, a, b) == .eq` or `!= .eq` used to test equality,
recommending `std.mem.eql(T, a, b)` or `!std.mem.eql(T, a, b)` instead.
<!-- /rule-docs:header -->

## Why it matters

`std.mem.order` performs a full lexicographical comparison to determine `<`/`>`
ordering, requiring shared-prefix byte-by-byte scanning even if `a.len !=
b.len`. In contrast, `std.mem.eql` first performs an $O(1)$ length check (`if
(a.len != b.len) return false;`), avoiding memory accesses entirely when lengths
differ, and uses vector-optimized equality comparisons. Testing for `.eq` order
is an unnecessary performance penalty.

## When it fires

Whenever checking whether two slices are equal or not equal using the `order`
comparison function.

<!-- rule-docs:footer (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
## Example

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn same(a: []const u8, b: []const u8) bool {
    return std.mem.order(u8, a, b) == .eq;
}
```
